core_summary: This chapter explores the rich variety of plant and animal life across different ecosystems. It categorizes plants by their stem growth habits (herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers, creepers) and examines how animals move using specialized bodily structures. It highlights morphological and physiological adaptations that enable plants and animals to thrive in desert, aquatic, mountain, and grassland habitats.
key_concepts: Categorization of plants into Herbs, Shrubs, Trees, Climbers, and Creepers based on stem character and branching.
Variations in animal locomotion mechanisms corresponding to terrestrial, aerial, and aquatic habitats.
Structural Adaptations: Webbed feet in ducks, streamlined bodies in fish, conical shapes in mountain trees, and spines in cacti.
Interdependence of flora and fauna within local biodiversity hotspots and guided nature walks.

key_terms.definition: The development of special physical features or behaviors that help an organism survive in its specific habitat.
The natural environment or home where an organism lives, grows, and reproduces.
The thick, main, hard woody stem of a tree that branches high above the ground.
A slender thread-like structure used by climber plants to wrap around external supports.

key_takeaways: Living organisms exhibit immense diversity in size, shape, stem structure, and movement.
Body structures are specialized to suit the physical demands of an organism's specific natural habitat.
Community knowledge and field observations enhance our understanding of regional flora and fauna.
